tasks.title: Per-cell condition-enrichment (relative likelihood) scoring on a cell graph
tasks.summary: Scores each cell by the local ratio of condition-specific densities in a cell embedding, so an analyst can see which cells lie in regions enriched for one condition, on one stated scale.
tasks.question: For each cell $i$, how strongly does the condition-specific density around $x_i$ favour condition 2 over condition 1, after smoothing over a cell graph? The inputs are a cell embedding (or a kNN graph built from it) and per-cell sample and condition labels. Each output is a balanced score $s_i \in [-1,1]$ defined in section 3. A correct answer recovers the planted local density ratio, is stable across graph settings, and flags no cells under sample-level nulls.

tasks.question: Which predefined cell types change in relative abundance between conditions when cells are nested in donors or libraries and shares sum to one within each sample? The input is a sample-by-type count table built from cell labels and sample IDs, with sample-level covariates. The output is, per type, a log-ratio effect against a reference (or an equivalent constraint), a p-value or posterior inclusion probability, and an FDR-controlled call. tasks.question: At which nodes of a cell-type hierarchy, built from clustering at several resolutions or from ordered author labels, do sample-level cell-type shares change between conditions? The inputs are sample-by-leaf counts and sample covariates. The outputs are node effects on the log-ratio scale to a reference leaf, with inclusion probabilities, FDR-controlled calls and a stability score across resolutions. A correct answer recovers planted node-level changes at the nominal false-call rate and gives the same calls at every resolution where the change is resolvable.

Inputs are a kNN graph over cells, a cell-to-sample map, the phenotype and covariates. Outputs are a global association p-value, a per-cell statistic with its FDR, and FDR-controlled cell calls. A correct answer takes the sample, not the cell, as the unit of replication and recovers planted associations with known truth.

tasks.title: Annotation and label-transfer confidence calibration and abstention
tasks.summary: Recalibrate an annotator's per-cell confidence on held-out donors or studies, measure how well it matches accuracy, and turn it into a label set or an abstention rule with a stated coverage.
tasks.question: Given an annotator's per-cell class probabilities or scores, and held-out cells with trusted labels from donors or studies it was not built on, does its top-label confidence match observed accuracy, can it be recalibrated, and which confidence threshold withholds the cells it cannot label reliably? A correct answer gives a confidence that is calibrated on new groups, and a frozen threshold or label set whose coverage and accuracy hold there.

tasks.title: Cell type name harmonization to Cell Ontology terms

tasks.question: Which Cell Ontology (CL) term, from a pinned release, does a free-text cell type label name, so that equivalent labels from different studies resolve to one identifier? The input is the set of unique label strings in one annotation column; the output is one CL identifier, its label and a match type per unique label, or an explicit unmapped flag. A correct answer names the term the author intended at the granularity the study used, and abstains when no single term fits.

tasks.title: Cluster-level cell type label assignment

tasks.question: Given a fixed partition of cells into clusters, which cell type best describes each cluster from its marker statistics or aggregated expression, and when is the evidence too weak to call a type? Inputs are the count and log-normalised matrices, the cluster labels, and a marker table or labelled reference restricted to tissue and species. Outputs are one label per cluster, a method-specific score, ranked alternatives and a called or unknown flag. A correct answer names the type holding most of the cluster's cells in the reference truth; Unknown counts as wrong in the benchmarks.

tasks.title: Consensus annotation across methods or annotators

tasks.question: Do aggregated labels from several annotators, or from marker and reference evidence, beat the best single annotator on held-out studies, and does the disagreement flag mark the cells that are wrong? Inputs are $M$ label columns over the same cells, optionally with per-call scores. A correct answer reports accuracy and macro-F1 against expert labels, coverage, and how well the flag ranks errors.

tasks.question: Given cells from two or more studies, each with its own author labels (free text, at different granularities), which label pairs denote the same population, a broader or narrower one, or a population specific to one study, and which harmonised label and parent does each cell receive? A correct answer matches the relations an expert would draw from the populations and gives the cells of one population the same harmonised label in every study. tasks.summary: Chooses t-SNE or UMAP hyperparameters for a fixed reference by scoring every candidate with label-free criteria, then writes the selected map with the scores that justify it.
tasks.question: Given the first $n$ principal components $X$ of a dataset and candidate values of perplexity or $n_{\text{neighbors}}$, `min_dist`, learning rate, early exaggeration and initialization, which setting gives a two-dimensional map that keeps the neighbourhoods of $X$ and reproduces across seeds, without judging the map by eye? The output is one map, the per-setting scores and the rule used. A correct answer ranks settings by neighbourhood faithfulness and stability, not by the spacing of clusters on the map.

tasks.title: Embedding of very large datasets
tasks.summary: Compute a two-dimensional map of $10^5$ to $10^7$ cells within a fixed memory budget by approximating the neighbour graph and the repulsive force, and measure how far the map departs from the exact method on subsamples where that method can be computed.
tasks.question: Can a two-dimensional map of $10^5$ to $10^7$ cells be computed in practical time and memory while keeping the neighbourhoods of the exact or full-data method? Input: a PCA matrix $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}$ (default $d=50$) with a time and memory budget, optionally a GPU. Output: coordinates $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 2}$, stage timings, peak memory and the stored affinity count. A correct answer means that the measured cost follows the complexity of the chosen algorithm and that local neighbourhoods agree with the exact method wherever it can be computed (section 8).

tasks.title: Local neighbourhood preservation of an embedding or reduced representation
tasks.summary: Score how well each cell's nearest neighbours in a reference representation stay nearest neighbours in a low-dimensional map, per cell and as global summaries that are corrected for chance.
tasks.question: Given a reference representation $X$ of $n$ cells (by default the first 50 principal components of normalised expression, or the full normalised layer), a low-dimensional map $Y$ of the same cells and neighbourhood sizes $k$: how many of each cell's $k$ nearest reference neighbours remain among its $k$ nearest map neighbours, and how far outside the neighbourhood do displaced neighbours fall? The output is a score per cell and $k$, plus global summaries over the scored cells, including the chance-corrected co-ranking curve $R_{NX}$. tasks.title: Out-of-sample placement of new cells on a fixed 2D map
tasks.summary: Place new cells on a fixed 2D reference map so that each lands where a joint re-embedding of reference and query would put it, and score each placement against the seed-to-seed spread of that joint target.
tasks.question: Given a fixed 2D map of reference cells, their PCA coordinates, and query cells in the same PCA space, where should each query cell be drawn, without changing the reference, so that its position matches where a joint re-embedding of reference and query would place it? A correct placement lies within the seed spread of that joint target, and the labels and novelty flags derived from it agree with held-out author annotation.

benchmarks.title: Placement fidelity against a joint re-embedding

tasks.title: Trajectory and branch preservation in a 2D layout
tasks.summary: Scores whether a 2D layout keeps a reference trajectory's geodesic order, branch sets and milestone topology, measured on the graph that the layout itself implies.
tasks.question: Does a two-dimensional layout keep a known trajectory intact, with cells ordered along each branch, branch membership preserved and branch points where the reference puts them, or does it cut the continuum into artificial clusters or merge branches? Inputs are the PCA coordinates and kNN graph of a dataset with a reference trajectory (simulated, or labelled by sampling time) and a 2D layout. The output is one score per layout, metric, dataset and seed. A good layout reproduces the reference geodesic order and milestone topology; the score says nothing about cluster sizes or global density.

tasks.title: Cell-type specificity enrichment of arbitrary gene lists
tasks.question: Which cell types in a single-cell reference specifically express a given gene list (differentially expressed, disease-associated or curated), after correcting for list length and expression-level confounding?

tasks.title: Replicate-aware differential activity of pathways, regulons and programs between conditions
tasks.summary: Test whether pathway, regulon or program activity differs between conditions within each cell type when donors or samples are the replicates, returning donor-level effects, standard errors, p-values and FDR calibrated by donor-label permutation.
tasks.question: Within one annotated cell type, does the activity of a pathway, TF regulon, gene program or metabolic pathway differ between conditions when donors or biological samples, not cells, are the replicates? Inputs are raw UMI counts with donor, cell-type and condition labels, optional covariates, and a gene-set or signed footprint resource. Per pathway and cell type the output is an effect, its standard error, a statistic, a p-value and a Benjamini-Hochberg FDR across pathways [R17]. tasks.title: Background universe and selection-bias correction for enrichment
tasks.question: Which background universe, and which correction for gene length, detection rate and annotation bias, gives calibrated enrichment p-values for marker and DE lists from scRNA-seq?

tasks.title: Over-representation analysis of marker or DE gene lists
tasks.summary: Tests whether a thresholded list of cluster-marker or differential-expression genes overlaps each predefined gene set more than chance allows, against an explicit background universe, and reports an odds ratio, fold enrichment, p-value and adjusted p-value for every set.
tasks.question: Which predefined gene sets contain more members of a thresholded foreground list (cluster markers or DE genes) than expected if the list were drawn at random from a stated background universe, and by how much? The input is a foreground list, a universe and a gene-set collection. The output is one row per set with the overlap and its genes, an odds ratio, a fold enrichment, a raw p-value and an adjusted p-value. A correct answer has p-values calibrated under the stated null and is read only relative to that universe.

benchmarks.title: Null calibration of the universe choice (proposed)

tasks.title: Pathway activity inference from signaling footprints
tasks.summary: Scores each sample or cell for signaling pathway activity by weighting the expression of pathway-responsive genes with signed footprint weights, and checks those scores against known perturbations.
tasks.question: Given normalised expression (bulk, pseudobulk or per cell) and a signed footprint that assigns each signaling pathway a set of responsive genes with weights, what is each pathway's activity in each sample or cell, and do the scores recover pathway perturbations? Input is log-normalised expression with gene symbols; output is a signed activity matrix, optionally with p-values. A correct answer ranks the perturbed pathway highest in held-out perturbation data at a stated false-positive rate, and is not driven by cell type, proliferation or library size.

benchmarks.title: Holland et al. 2020 in silico benchmark (pathway arm)

tasks.title: Curated pathway gene-set and signed footprint resource construction
tasks.summary: Builds one harmonised table of pathway members, signs and weights from curated and perturbation-derived sources, prunes redundant sets, and ranks the resulting collections by how well they recover held-out pathway perturbations.
tasks.question: Which genes, signs and weights belong in a reusable pathway resource, and which collection, after size and overlap pruning, gives activity estimates that best recover known pathway perturbations? Inputs are curated or perturbation-derived sources, a gene universe and a perturbation compendium with study labels. Outputs are a resource table and a recovery score per resource. A correct answer ranks collections on held-out perturbations and states the pruning and sign convention behind each rank.

benchmarks.title: Resource consistency and pruning stability (proposed, consistency rather than accuracy)

tasks.title: Per-cell gene set activity scoring (covariate-robust, null-calibrated)
tasks.summary: Scores every cell for a predefined, optionally signed, gene set, with a rank-based heuristic as the default and a proposed null-calibrated, covariate-aware model as the candidate improvement.
tasks.question: For each cell $c$ and each gene set $G$ with up members $G^+$ and optional down members $G^-$, what is the activity $S_c(G)$ such that cells rank by their true activity and the score stays independent of set size, member detection rate, depth, cell cycle and QC covariates? The input is a cells-by-genes count or log-normalised matrix and a gene-set collection. The output is a cells-by-sets matrix, optional binary calls and optional matched-null z-scores. No accepted per-cell ground truth exists, so a correct answer is judged against planted activity, perturbation labels and held-out annotations

tasks.title: Preranked gene set enrichment on gene-level statistics
tasks.summary: Tests whether the members of a gene set sit at the extremes of a genome-wide ranking of one signed gene-level statistic, returning a running-sum score, a sign-matched normalised score, a permutation p-value and a set-level FDR for each cell type and contrast.
tasks.question: Is a gene set concentrated at the top or bottom of a genome-wide ranking of one signed statistic, such as the donor-level pseudobulk t-statistic for one cell type and one contrast? The input is one value per gene and a gene-set collection with size limits. The output per set is an enrichment score (ES), a normalised enrichment score (NES), a sign-matched p-value, a Benjamini-Hochberg q-value and leading-edge genes. A correct answer uses the estimands of section 3, gives p-values calibrated under a donor-level null, and recovers planted shifts (B3).

tasks.title: Sample-level and pseudobulk pathway activity scoring
tasks.summary: Scores each sample, or each cell-type-by-sample pseudobulk group, against each gene set from a normalized sample-by-gene layer, returning one set score per sample together with the member coverage behind it.
tasks.question: For each sample or pseudobulk group, what is the activity of each gene set, so that samples can be compared on pathway-level variables? Inputs are a normalized sample-by-gene layer and a named gene-set collection with optional signs or weights; the output is a sample-by-set score matrix with per-set coverage. A correct answer orders samples by planted activity, gives a null for random matched sets that is centred and uncorrelated with library size, and, for per-sample methods, does not change when other samples are added.

tasks.title: Label-free cluster validity indices

tasks.question: Given one embedding of a set of cells and candidate partitions of those cells, do internal geometric indices rank the partitions, and the granularities they represent, in the same order as their biological agreement, when no reference labels exist? Inputs are the embedding and one labelling per candidate. Outputs are one score per index per partition, per-cell silhouette, and a flag stating whether the best partition lies inside the swept range and whether silhouette supports it. tasks.title: Expression-based label-free cluster purity and heterogeneity
tasks.summary: Scores each cluster of a candidate partition for expression heterogeneity with ROGUE, SCCAF or phiclust, flags likely mixtures once calibrated, and reports how the scores change with clustering granularity.
tasks.question: Given a normalised count matrix and one or more candidate cluster partitions, which clusters mix several expression states, and how homogeneous is each cluster? The output is a per-cluster score (ROGUE lies in $(0,1]$, higher is purer), a mixed-cluster flag once calibrated, and a partition-level summary across resolutions. A correct answer flags clusters that combine two populations in mixtures of known composition and leaves single-population clusters unflagged.

benchmarks.title: Cell-line mixtures: pure versus mixed clusters

tasks.title: Over-correction after batch or covariate removal
tasks.summary: Detects whether a batch-correction, integration or covariate-regression step has removed condition-level differential expression, cell-type structure or marker separation that was present before correction, and reports the loss as a retention score checked against planted truth.
tasks.question: Given raw counts, donor, batch, condition and cell-type labels, an uncorrected embedding, and a corrected embedding or corrected expression matrix, how much of the pre-correction condition biology survives correction? The output is the sets of differential genes before and after correction, a retention fraction $R\in[0,1]$, a sign concordance $\rho$, an over-correction score $O=1-R$, and kNN-purity and marker readouts. A correct answer keeps the pre-correction direction and significance of condition effects while removing the batch effect as far as the batch-only design allows.

tasks.question: Given a multi-batch count matrix with batch labels, optionally coarse lineage labels, and a target size $K$, which $K$ genes should every batch share before integration? A correct answer keeps genes whose structure is shared within batches, discounts genes whose variation is only between batches, and keeps markers of populations present in one batch. The answer is judged by the integration it produces: batch removal, biological conservation and query mapping.

tasks.title: Unsupervised highly variable gene selection for clustering and embedding
tasks.summary: Choose the few thousand genes that feed PCA, neighbour graphs and clustering by scoring each gene against a technical null, with a model-based default and the published selectors kept as comparators.
tasks.question: Given a cells-by-genes matrix (raw UMI counts for the count-based statistics, log-normalised values for the dispersion and scran flavours) and a target size $N$, which $N$ genes, ranked by a per-gene variability, deviance or residual statistic, best preserve cell-type structure after PCA, neighbour-graph construction and clustering? tasks.title: Choosing how many features to keep
tasks.summary: Choose how many top-ranked genes feed PCA, neighbour graphs and integration, by a fixed count kept as the published comparator or by a plateau rule over a declared grid scored against author labels.
tasks.question: Given a gene ranking from any selector, the count matrix and a downstream task (integration, reference mapping, classification or unseen-population detection), how many top-ranked genes $N$ should be kept, and does one rule for $N$ hold across datasets? The output is an integer $N$ or a stopping rule, with the downstream score as a function of $N$. A correct answer is a rule whose chosen $N$ scores within a declared tolerance of the best value on a declared grid, on datasets that did not inform the choice [R1]. The proxies are author labels and simulated planted structure [R2].

tasks.summary: Embed a labelled dataset with a frozen foundation model, with no training on the target, and test against HVG-PCA and scVI whether the embedding separates expert cell types at least as well.
tasks.question: Does a frozen pretrained cell embedding, used with no task-specific training, separate expert-labelled cell types at least as well as a baseline embedding computed on the same cells? The input is raw counts of a labelled dataset that the model did not train on, the frozen checkpoint with its gene vocabulary, and expert labels used only for scoring. The output is one embedding per cell, scored by Leiden clustering and neighbourhood measures against the labels with ARI, NMI, cell-type ASW and cLISI. tasks.question: Does a gene show allelic imbalance or monoallelic expression in a cell type (or in individual cells), given sparse, dropout-prone allele counts at heterozygous sites?

tasks.title: Cell-type-specific cis-eQTL mapping and cross-cell-type effect sharing
tasks.summary: For each cell type, tests whether common variants near a gene shift its donor-level expression, then shares the estimated effects across cell types by empirical Bayes.
tasks.question: Which common variants in the cis window of a gene are associated with that gene's donor-level expression within each cell type, and how much of each effect is shared across cell types? Inputs are donor genotype dosages, donor-by-cell-type pseudobulk (or cell-level counts with donor labels) and donor covariates. Outputs are per-cell-type effects, standard errors, p-values and q-values, plus shrunken multi-context effects. A correct answer is an effect that holds in independent donors and matches the truth defined in section 8.

tasks.title: Clonal and subclonal grouping from genotype-derived cell features
tasks.summary: Groups tumour cells into clones, and arranges the clones into a tree where the method provides one, from copy-number states inferred from expression, phased allele counts or heteroplasmic mtDNA variants.
tasks.question: Given per-cell copy-number states, allele counts or mtDNA alternate and total counts from upstream variant tasks, which cells share a clone, and how are the clones nested? The output is a clone label and posterior per cell, plus a rooted clone tree where the method gives one. A correct answer groups tumour cells into the clones an independent DNA or lineage-barcode assay identifies, with each descendant carrying its ancestor's copy-number events.

tasks.title: Copy-number inference from scRNA-seq expression
tasks.summary: Infers, for each cell and genomic segment, whether total copy number is lost, neutral or gained relative to normal reference cells, using expression ordered along the genome, and uses allele counts where supplied to resolve loss of heterozygosity.
tasks.question: Given gene-by-cell UMI counts with gene coordinates and a normal reference (or an internal baseline), which chromosomal segments are lost or gained in each cell, at arm or segment scale? The output is a cell-by-segment state, a score and, for HMM callers, posterior probabilities; a correct answer matches the total copy number that DNA-based measurements of the same tumour report at the segment scale that expression resolves, and copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity or the haplotype of a gain needs allele counts.

tasks.title: Differential GRN, regulon and co-expression rewiring between conditions or cell types
tasks.summary: Test which gene pairs, TF-target edges or regulon activities change their dependence between two conditions beyond their change in mean expression, using donors as the unit of replication.
tasks.question: Given raw UMI counts with donor, condition and cell-type labels, which gene pairs, TF-target edges or regulons have a relationship that differs between two conditions more than their mean levels explain? The outputs are, for each tested pair or regulon, a signed difference (condition two minus condition one), a donor-permutation p-value and a Benjamini–Hochberg q-value. A correct answer keeps its false-positive rate near nominal when donor labels are shuffled within a condition [R1].

tasks.question: Given RNA counts and a peak-by-cell ATAC matrix measured on the same cells, a peak set, gene annotations and a versioned motif database, which accessible regions carrying which TF motifs link each TF to which target genes, and what is each eRegulon's activity in each cell? The outputs are region-gene links, TF-region motif assignments, signed eRegulons (TF, region set, target genes) and a cells-by-eRegulons activity matrix. A correct answer is a set of hypotheses that predicts held-out region-level or perturbation-level evidence, not a single network.

tasks.title: Curated TF-target prior network (regulon resource) construction
tasks.summary: Build a signed, confidence-annotated table of transcription factor (TF) to target-gene edges from curated sources, so that TF activity scoring and regulator analysis share one reproducible prior.
tasks.question: Which TF-to-target edges, with what sign and what confidence, belong in a reusable regulon resource for a given species? A correct resource ranks perturbed TFs first when its edges drive TF activity estimates in perturbation experiments [R1][R3].

tasks.question: Given a log-normalised expression matrix (cells or pseudobulk samples by genes) and a prior table of signed TF-target regulons, what is the activity of each TF in each observation? A correct answer gives the expected sign and rank for TFs that were knocked down or overexpressed in matched experiments, and scores that do not track library size or detection rate. Outputs are an observation-by-TF score matrix, optional p-values and binary top-fraction calls [R1][R2].

tasks.question: For one cell population with a log-normalised matrix $X$ over $n$ cells and a candidate regulator set $\mathcal R$ of annotated TFs, which ordered pairs (TF $i$, target $j$) receive the highest scores, and do those scores rank reference-network edges above non-edges? The output is a weighted directed edge list over all candidate pairs, with no threshold. A correct answer ranks reference edges highly, is reproducible across seeds, and is read as a conditional association, not an intervention.

tasks.title: Count-matrix processing-state detection
tasks.summary: Labels a stored expression matrix as raw counts, normalized, log1p, scaled, z-scored, Pearson residuals or unresolved non-integer data from its values alone, and flags any conflict with the declared state.
tasks.question: Given a stored cells-by-genes matrix $Y$ (dense or sparse, whole or one layer) and optionally the state its metadata declares or a downstream method requires, which processing state produced its values: raw UMI counts, library-size normalized values, a shifted logarithm, scaled, z-scored or analytic Pearson residuals, or non-integer non-negative data that the values cannot resolve? The output is one label per matrix, its supporting statistics, and a conflict flag against the declared state. A correct label is the state that generated the values, which is known only for planted data (section 8)

tasks.title: Gene identifier and symbol mapping

A correct answer assigns a feature to a gene only when its candidate set in that release has exactly one member; every other case is flagged rather than guessed.

A correct answer matches blind expert curation on the value and its span, and returns null rather than a guess when the record does not state the field. Input: characteristics fields, titles, descriptions and file names. Output: one normalised row per sample.

tasks.title: Matrix and metadata integrity checks

tasks.title: Sample metadata to ontology term mapping

The input is the raw field values, a schema identifier and the release pins. The output is, per field, a validated term ID with its label, match type, calibrated confidence and curation flag. A correct answer names the term the value denotes within the allowed range, or abstains. Age and sex are excluded (§10).

tasks.title: Metadata conformance to a community schema

tasks.title: Post-clustering inference with valid p-values (double-dipping correction)
tasks.summary: Test whether genes differ between clusters that were defined from the same counts, reporting per-gene p-values and BH q-values whose false positive rate stays at the nominal level after the clustering step.
tasks.question: Are genes that differ between clusters still significant when the clusters were defined from the same counts, once that clustering step is accounted for? The input is a cell-by-gene UMI matrix and cluster labels computed from it, or the procedure that produced them. The output is a per-gene p-value and a Benjamini-Hochberg q-value for each cluster contrast. A correct answer keeps the false positive rate at the nominal level under the null of no true mean difference between the clusters the algorithm returns.

benchmarks.title: Null type I error and p-value uniformity under one population
Planted between-cluster difference: power and realised FDR

tasks.title: Type I error and p-value calibration of single-cell tests under replicate-respecting nulls
tasks.summary: Measure whether a single-cell differential expression test keeps its nominal false-positive rate and uniform p-values when no condition effect exists, using nulls that treat donors (not cells) as the replicate, and report a calibration verdict for each method and cell type.
tasks.question: When donors are the true sampling units and no condition effect exists, does a single-cell test keep its nominal false-positive rate at each level $\alpha$ and give uniform p-values, or does treating cells as replicates inflate its calls? The input is a raw count matrix with donor, condition and cell-type labels, the methods to evaluate and a null construction that keeps the donor hierarchy. tasks.title: Sequencing depth and cell-number sufficiency for cell-type and marker recovery
tasks.question: How many reads (or UMIs) per cell and how many cells are needed for a stated analysis goal (broad cell-type recovery, marker-gene detection, cluster stability, gene-level estimates) before additional depth stops improving it, and can that saturation point be predicted from a pilot or shallow dataset?

tasks.title: Circadian phase inference from single-cell and pseudobulk transcriptomes
tasks.question: What time of day (circadian phase on a 24 h circle) does each cell, cell type or pseudobulk sample correspond to, estimated from its transcriptome alone, and which genes are phase-informative or rhythmic?

tasks.title: Dose-response modelling of single-cell expression
tasks.question: How does each gene's or cell state's expression change with perturbation dose, and what potency, threshold or saturation dose defines the response?

tasks.title: Longitudinal time-effect differential expression with repeated measures
tasks.question: Which genes change over real sampling time (three or more ordered time points, or a continuous time covariate) within the same donors or replicates, with inference done at the donor or replicate level and the temporal shape of the change estimated?

tasks.title: Supervised ordering of cells or samples by sampling time
tasks.question: Can an ordinal or regression model trained on labelled sampling times or stages predict the time of held-out cells or samples, and which genes drive that ordering?

tasks.title: Temporal expression profile clustering and onset/peak timing
tasks.question: Which genes share the same temporal response profile across ordered real time points after a stimulus or perturbation, and what are their onset and peak times?

tasks.title: Transcriptional age prediction (single-cell aging clock)
tasks.question: How accurately does a cell-type-resolved expression profile predict chronological age in held-out donors or animals, and do residuals from predicted age (age acceleration) reflect biology rather than composition, donor leakage or batch?

tasks.title: Branch point localisation and cell-to-branch assignment
tasks.summary: Estimates where lineages split along a trajectory and assigns each cell to a branch, as hard labels, soft weights or fate probabilities, scored by split position and by branch agreement.
tasks.question: Where along a trajectory do lineages split, and which branch does each cell belong to? Inputs are a trajectory graph or per-lineage pseudotime, the expression embedding, a required root cell and optional terminal states. Outputs are branch points (pseudotime and graph node), a hard label or soft weights per cell, and branch-specific pseudotime. A correct answer places each split at the true fork time and assigns each cell to the branch its true fate follows.

tasks.title: Differential progression, topology and fate selection between conditions
tasks.question: Along a shared trajectory, do conditions differ in topology, in how far cells progress along pseudotime, or in the proportion of cells choosing each lineage?

tasks.title: Cell-fate probability estimation
tasks.summary: Estimates, for each cell, the probability of reaching each terminal state from a transition structure, and tests those probabilities against fates measured independently of expression.
tasks.question: For each cell, what is the probability that its descendants reach each terminal state, and do these probabilities match fates measured independently of the transcriptome? Inputs are a kNN graph or velocity or time-course snapshots, terminal states (given or inferred) and an optional root. Outputs are a cells-by-terminal-states matrix whose rows sum to one, with per-cell entropy and argmax. A correct answer matches clonal descendant fractions where lineage barcodes exist, because snapshot expression alone does not determine fate probabilities [R1].

tasks.title: Gene expression shape classes and switch timing along pseudotime
tasks.question: Which shape class (constant, monotone, transient, switch-like) does each gene follow along pseudotime, at which pseudotime does a switch or peak occur, and in what order do genes switch on or off?

tasks.title: Pseudotime-associated and lineage-specific differential expression
tasks.summary: Tests, for each gene, whether its expression changes along pseudotime, differs between lineages or branches, or changes from lineage start to end, using negative-binomial models with false discovery control.
tasks.question: Which genes change along pseudotime, differ between lineages at matched progression, or differ between the start and end of a lineage? Inputs are raw counts, one pseudotime per cell, optional lineage weights and optional labels. Outputs are a statistic, p-value and FDR per gene, and fitted expression curves. A correct answer calls a gene only when its trend departs from the null trend beyond chance, with FDR controlled, and with pseudotime treated as estimated rather than exact.

tasks.title: Pseudotime ordering along a lineage
tasks.summary: Assigns each cell a scalar progress value along one lineage, oriented by a required root cell, using diffusion, geodesic or curve-projection distances.
tasks.question: Does a per-cell pseudotime rank cells in their true order of developmental or response progress along one lineage, with the root at the start? Inputs are an embedding (PCA by default), a kNN graph, a root cell and optional cluster labels. Output is one real value per cell per lineage. A correct answer is a monotone ranking of cells by true progress, with the root at the start.

tasks.title: Pseudotime and trajectory uncertainty quantification
tasks.question: How uncertain is each cell's pseudotime and branch assignment, and how stable is the inferred topology under resampling, parameter choice or method choice?

tasks.title: Root or start-state identification
tasks.summary: Chooses the source cell or cluster of a developmental process, which fixes the origin and direction of pseudotime. The default is an anchored choice that is cross-checked against potency and graph criteria.
tasks.question: Which cell or cluster is the source (progenitor) state of the process, so that pseudotime starts at the origin and points in the right direction? Inputs are an embedding and a kNN graph, counts for a gene-count potency score, optional cluster labels, and an optional anchor cell or cluster. Outputs are ranked root candidates and one selected root cell with its cluster. A correct answer is a cell of the source state, as defined by the benchmarks in section 8.

benchmarks.title: Planted branching simulation with known generation index

tasks.title: Spatial pseudotime and trajectory inference over tissue coordinates
tasks.question: Given spatial transcriptomics sections (single or time-series), can pseudotime, trajectories and spot/cell-to-spot/cell lineage relations be inferred that respect tissue geometry and recover known developmental order or ancestor-descendant relationships, beyond what expression-only trajectory inference gives?

tasks.title: Spatially informed pseudotime and spatiotemporal trajectory inference
tasks.question: Can pseudotime or developmental flow be inferred on spatial data so that it is spatially coherent and agrees with known tissue axes or sampled stages, including coupling between sections of successive stages?

tasks.title: Initial and terminal state (macrostate) identification
tasks.summary: Finds the endpoints of a cell-state process and the cells that belong to each, from a directed transition kernel, and scores the calls on annotated endpoints, lineage fates and planted simulations.
tasks.question: Given a kNN graph on an embedding, an optional direction (pseudotime) and an optional root cell, which macrostates are the terminal and initial states of the process, and which cells belong to each? Outputs are hard terminal labels, soft memberships and initial-state weights. A correct answer recovers the endpoints the sampled process reaches and does not call sampling edges or arrested states terminal.

benchmarks.title: dynverse milestone evaluation with end states (published benchmark, terminal use extended)

tasks.title: Trajectory topology inference
tasks.summary: Infers the graph of milestones that a cell population traces in an embedding, and gives each cell soft positions on that graph.
tasks.question: What graph (nodes, edges, branch points, endpoints, loops and disconnected components) best describes the state space of a continuously changing or responding population in a low-dimensional embedding, and where does each cell sit on that graph? The inputs are an embedding of normalised expression, optional cluster labels and an optional start cell. The outputs are a milestone network and per-cell milestone percentages. A correct answer matches the planted or reference topology class and the true cell positions, as scored in section 8.

tasks.title: Trajectory alignment across conditions, datasets or species
tasks.question: What is the correspondence between the pseudotime axes of two or more trajectories (conditions, batches, donors or species), and where do their timing or branch choices diverge?

tasks.title: Trajectory presence and suitability test before trajectory inference
tasks.question: Does the cell-state distribution contain continuous, lineage-like structure that supports trajectory inference at all, as opposed to discrete clusters or unstructured noise, and which trajectory properties are stable across analysis choices?

tasks.title: Per-gene kinetics and RNA velocity estimation from spliced and unspliced counts
tasks.summary: Fits a two-pool kinetic model to each gene's spliced and unspliced counts and returns degradation ratios and per-cell velocity, with the steady-state and dynamical methods of the literature kept as comparators.
tasks.question: What transcription, splicing and degradation rates per gene, and what per-cell velocity (the instantaneous rate of change of spliced abundance), best explain observed spliced and unspliced UMI counts? The input is a cells-by-genes pair of spliced and unspliced matrices, with a kNN graph for smoothing. The output is a per-gene kinetic table and a cells-by-genes velocity matrix. A correct answer recovers ratios of rates and the direction of velocity; absolute rates and the time origin are not identifiable from counts (section 3).

benchmarks.title: Gene-level degradation rates against labelling-derived rates

tasks.title: Latent time and temporal ordering from splicing dynamics
tasks.summary: Assigns each cell a latent time on one shared clock from fitted splicing kinetics, and checks the cell ordering against planted or recorded time.
tasks.question: Where does each cell lie along a differentiation or response process, as implied by the splicing kinetics of its genes? Inputs are raw spliced and unspliced counts, a kNN graph and one root cell that marks the start of the process. Outputs are a per-cell latent time on a shared scale and, for kinetic methods, gene-wise fitted times. A correct answer ranks cells as the true process does and places the start at the root. The absolute scale is a convention, so correctness is a claim about ranks.

tasks.title: RNA synthesis and degradation rates from metabolic labelling
tasks.question: What per-gene synthesis and degradation rates, or half-lives, are supported by new-versus-old RNA counts from labelling time courses or pulse-chase designs?

tasks.title: Chromatin-aware multiome RNA velocity
tasks.question: Does modelling chromatin accessibility ahead of transcription in paired multiome data improve per-gene kinetics, velocity direction or fate prediction relative to RNA-only velocity?

tasks.title: New versus old RNA quantification from metabolic labelling
tasks.question: Which reads, UMIs or transcripts in each cell derive from RNA synthesised during the labelling window versus pre-existing RNA?

tasks.title: Optimal-transport coupling of unpaired time-point snapshots
tasks.question: Given unpaired time-course snapshots without lineage barcodes, which cells at one time point are the likely ancestors or descendants of cells at the next, and at what growth rates?

tasks.title: Population dynamics interpolation and held-out time-point prediction
tasks.question: Can the cell-state distribution at an unobserved time point be predicted from neighbouring snapshots by a model of population-level dynamics?

tasks.title: Transcriptional burst kinetics from single-cell count distributions
tasks.question: What burst frequency, burst size and degradation (or promoter switching) parameters of a stochastic transcription model best explain each gene's cell-to-cell UMI count distribution once technical noise and capture efficiency are separated from biological stochasticity, and which of these parameters are practically identifiable from a snapshot?

tasks.title: Continuous vector-field reconstruction and fixed-point analysis
tasks.question: What continuous vector field over expression or latent space is consistent with the observed velocities, and where are its attractors, saddle points and transition paths?

tasks.title: Velocity gene selection and steady-state assumption check
tasks.question: For which genes or cells is the velocity model's assumption (for example steady state or shared kinetics) violated or the signal too weak, so that velocity is biased, and which gene set should be kept?

tasks.title: Velocity-based cell-to-cell transition graph and embedding projection
tasks.summary: Converts per-cell RNA velocity and a neighbour graph into a row-stochastic matrix of likely next cells and into projected 2D arrows, keeping published kernels as comparators.
tasks.question: Given each cell's velocity vector and its candidate neighbours, which neighbours does the cell move toward and with what probability, and does the resulting directed graph point from earlier to later states? Inputs are the velocity matrix, the expression representation, a kNN graph and an optional 2D embedding; outputs are a row-stochastic transition matrix and arrows projected onto the embedding. A correct answer ranks the neighbours a cell moves toward above those it moves away from, and its direction agrees with external time or lineage where such information exists.

tasks.title: Per-cell velocity uncertainty and robustness
tasks.question: How reliable is each cell's inferred velocity direction under noise, gene filtering, preprocessing and model choice, and which cells or regions should be flagged as unreliable?
